title: Prompt eviction strategy and cost/latency tradeoffs with Lyra Analytics
summary: Technical deep dive on prompt/kv eviction strategies for multi-tenant prompt cache. Discussed hit-rate measurement, eviction policies (LRU, LFU, TTL), tenant-aware sharding, cost vs latency tradeoffs, correctness risks for shared KV cache, and on-prem/VPC implications. Agreed to run 2-week pilot with 500k requests/day workload and share benchmark spreadsheet + security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-08 14:30 UTC | Duration 65m | Recording: Zoom | Attendees: Maya, Diego, Priya (Redwood); Samir, Aisha, Tom, Nora (Lyra)

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick agenda — we want to walk through Lyra's current prompt caching patterns, show how Redwood's KV/prompt cache can be configured, and surface tradeoffs around eviction and multi-tenant safety. Then we can land on pilot config.

[00:18] Samir (Lyra): Yeah thanks. High level, our use case is a customer-facing insights assistant. We see lots of repeated prefixes — same system prompts, repeated user contexts — so hoping caching gives meaningful token cost savings and latency improvements.

[00:35] Diego (SE): Great. First, can you share approximate numbers — rps, unique prompts per hour, distribution? That helps pick cache key scheme.

[00:48] Aisha (Lyra): Rough numbers: 500 requests per second at peak, avg 300k req/day. But unique prompt templates are a long tail — maybe 50k unique prompt fingerprints per day. We tried coarse hashing to reduce uniqueness but worried about collisions.

[01:10] Priya (Redwood): That's helpful. Two immediate knobs: key granularity and eviction policy. Key granularity: do you cache whole prompt+system+history, or just system+intent? The hit-rate hinges on that.

[01:28] Nora (Product): Can you clarify "prompt fingerprint"? I think we call it template id internally. Sometimes the user-specific bits (like name/placeholders) make keys different.

[01:40] Diego: Prompt fingerprinting is typically normalized text -> deterministic hash. But you can also do templated keys: replace placeholders with tokens so identical templates map together. That reduces cardinality.

[01:55] Tom (SRE): Our privacy/legal folks want guarantees that user-identifying PII is not stored in cache. How does that play with templating?

[02:05] Priya: We recommend template extraction at client-side or edge before sending to cache. Redwood can accept a "template_id" header that we use as cache key; the payload still goes to the model but the cache key doesn't contain PII. For private deployment we can enforce that at the VPC boundary.

[02:28] Samir: Ok. Eviction — we tried LRU but saw cache thrash because of a big tail. Any other strategies?

[02:38] Diego: Common options: LRU, LFU, TinyLFU (approx frequency-based), TTL-based expiry, and hybrid: frequency + recency. For long-tail workloads, LFU or TinyLFU reduces thrash from one-off peaks. But LFU needs a compact frequency sketch to be efficient.

[02:58] Maya: Also important is admission policy — whether to insert large responses into cache. We sometimes avoid caching large completion outputs because cost of storing plus eviction pressure outweigh benefits.

[03:15] Aisha: How do you measure hit rate realistically? Our analytics currently overstates hits because the measurement is at the app layer, not at the serving runtime.

[03:25] Diego: Instrument at the runtime layer. Redwood emits token-level metrics: cache_lookup_attempts, cache_hits, hit_latency, and hit_response_size. You can correlate with app-level logs to reconcile. We'll provide dashboards.

[03:40] Nora: Any gotchas with batching? We batch small requests to GPUs for throughput — does that change cache behavior?

[03:48] Priya: Yes. Batching interacts with cache in two ways: 1) If you have a batch of independent requests and only some hit the cache, we avoid executing model for hit ones and only run for misses, but batching windows can add a small extra latency if you wait to form batches. 2) For KV (prefix) caches, if multiple requests reuse same KV state, batching can actually improve efficiency by reusing cached KV across batch sequence steps. But it complicates measuring per-request latency.

[04:20] Samir: What about multi-tenant safety? We don't want one tenant's hot keys to evict another's valuable entries.

[04:30] Diego: Two approaches: strong isolation — per-tenant caches (sharded) — or soft isolation — global cache with tenant-aware admission + quotas. Per-tenant sharding guarantees no cross-tenant eviction but at cost of fragmentation (cold tenants get less effective cache). Soft isolation keeps high utilization but needs eviction quotas and per-tenant weight adjustments.

[04:56] Tom: On private deploy we'll probably want per-tenant pools because our SLAs require predictable tail latency.

[05:04] Maya: Right — Dedicated or Private gives you options. For multi-tenant public hosting, we usually recommend hashed sharding with tenanted buckets: e.g., allocate N shards per tenant proportionate to expected qps plus an overflow pool. That gives both isolation and global efficiency.

[05:22] Aisha: Hash collisions — earlier someone mentioned collisions being a risk. How do you mitigate false positives where a different prompt hashes to same key?

[05:30] Diego: Use strong hash (SHA256) + store a short fingerprint in the entry to validate. If mismatch, treat as miss. Also keep versioned key namespaces when you change normalization rules. Collisions at SHA256 are negligible but malformed normalization can lead to logical collisions.

[05:50] Nora: You mentioned TTLs — how to pick TTL for templates that change often? We have templates that are A/B tested every day.

[05:58] Priya: For frequently changing templates, use short TTLs (minutes-hours) and add manual invalidation APIs. Redwood supports explicit cache invalidation by template_id and global prefixes, and we can wire that to your CI/CD so deployments invalidate cache keys related to changed templates.

[06:20] Samir: Let's talk numbers — if we do templating + a TinyLFU with per-tenant shards, what hit rate should we expect?

[06:28] Diego: With your reported 50k unique templates/day and templating reducing cardinality by 10x, you'd be at ~5k hot keys. With TinyLFU and a working set sized to hold 5k entries, hit rates in the 45-65% range aren’t unrealistic. But depends on request skew — Pareto/Zipf distributions are common.

[06:50] Maya: Key to cost savings is token-level cache reuse — for completions that reuse prefixes, even a 50% hit rate on prefix tokens reduces per-request token generation significantly. We'll model cost both token and latency.

[07:10] Tom: Quantization — you had mentioned that quantized models can affect cacheability?

[07:16] Diego: Quantization normally affects runtime and model output determinism slightly. For KV/prefix caches, the cache stores activations or KV states, which are dependent on model precision. So a cache entry for FP16 model isn't compatible with an INT8 quantized variant. That means if you plan to fall back to quantized variants to save cost, you need separate cache namespaces per quantization profile or convert/rehydrate cache entries, which is complex.

[07:45] Aisha: So in a mixed environment we'd need to route all similar requests to the same model variant to keep cache hits?

[07:52] Priya: Exactly. Smart routing policy can keep hot keys on the high-precision variant for latency-sensitive traffic, while low-priority traffic goes to quantized models with separate caches. Redwood supports model-variant tagging for cache compatibility.

[08:10] Samir: Any thoughts on admission filtering to avoid storing noisy entries?

[08:16] Diego: Admission can check response size, frequency (e.g., only insert if seen > N times in a short window), or estimated token-savings threshold. TinyLFU inherently biases toward frequent items, but admission filters reduce write amplification.

[08:36] Nora: Could we run a dry run instrumenting only (no caching) to estimate potential savings?

[08:42] Maya: Yes — we recommend a "shadow cache" mode where runtime evaluates lookups and logs hypothetical hits without serving them. That gives conservative hit-rate estimates without risk. We can run shadow for 7-14 days to collect distribution.

[09:00] Aisha: That ties to instrumentation — what exact logs do you need?

[09:05] Diego: Ideally: normalized_template_id, request_timestamp, token_count, response_size, model_variant, tenant_id, and whether templating was applied. If you can't send full text, send hashed fingerprints. If on-prem, we can provide collectors.

[09:24] Tom: For VPC/on-prem we have egress and storage constraints — how big is the cache and where does it live?

[09:30] Priya: Cache can be in-memory on the serving nodes or backed by a fast distributed store (e.g., Redis with local LRU warm caches). For private deployments we usually size in-memory KV cache to fit working set; if memory is constrained, use sharded Redis with local LRU caches. We'll provide sizing guidance.

[09:52] Samir: Any security concerns if we use shared Redis for multiple tenants?

[09:58] Diego: You must ensure encryption in transit, per-tenant namespaces, and strict ACLs. For sensitive workloads we recommend private deploy with HSM/KMS and zero-persist mode for certain fields. Also consider field-level masking: never store raw PII in cache values.

[10:18] Nora: How to run the pilot? What's minimal scope?

[10:22] Maya: Pilot scope we propose: 2-week shadow-caching run + 2-week live pilot on a small percentage of traffic (10-20%) with templating and tenant shard config. Success metrics: token cost reduction %, median and 99th latency change, and no correctness regressions in 0.1% of responses.

[10:40] Samir: Sounds good. Any pitfalls to watch for?

[10:43] Diego: Watch cache invalidation alignment with A/B rollouts (staleness), model-variant incompatibilities, and batch-wait latencies. Also be careful about tenant imbalance — monitor per-tenant hit rates and eviction churn.

[11:00] Aisha: On correctness: sometimes caching prefixes for conversational state can leak context across users if keys are wrong. How do you prevent that?

[11:09] Priya: Strict key construction: include explicit tenant_id and conversation_id scoping fields in the cache key, or avoid caching any per-user state. For shared system prompts it's safe; for user-specific history we typically don't cache unless it's sanitized.

[11:28] Tom: Let's talk about cost modeling — our finance team asks for dollar savings estimates.

[11:34] Maya: We'll produce a simple model: baseline tokens generated per day * model cost per token - expected tokens generated after caching * cost. We'll give multiple scenarios (conservative, expected, optimistic) based on shadow-run hit rates. Also show GPU throughput/slot improvements that reduce infra cost.

[11:58] Nora: Any benchmarks you can share from similar customers?

[12:02] Priya: High-level only: a SaaS customer with templating + TinyLFU saw ~40% token reduction and 20-30% median latency improvement. We can share anonymized graphs.

[12:18] Samir: For Lyra, we will definitely want tenant sharding. We prefer isolation and predictability.

[12:26] Diego: Ok — so pilot config: per-tenant hash shards sized by errored estimate: we'll propose per-tenant initial shard count and overflow pool. We'll include TinyLFU + TTL 6 hours + admission filter (min frequency 3 hits in 1h) for the pilot.

[12:44] Aisha: How do you tune shard counts over time?

[12:48] Diego: Auto-rebalancer: periodically (daily) compute working-set size per tenant and reassign shard weights. We can do this slowly to avoid thrash. Also provide metrics to suggest manual adjustments.

[13:05] Tom: If we decide to use quantization on weekends for cost savings, how do we avoid cache fragmentation?

[13:13] Priya: Use model-variant tagging as mentioned and keep separate caches. For weekend quantization you could accept lower cache hit reuse because cache namespaces are different; alternatively keep a "warm" hot-key set pinned on FP16 nodes while routing cold traffic to quantized nodes.

[13:32] Maya: Quick note on eviction debugging: Redwood exposes per-shard eviction counters, eviction reasons, and a top-churn key feed to identify noisy templates to either increase TTL or exclude from cache.

[13:46] Samir: That top-churn feed would be super helpful for product to tune templates.

[13:50] Diego: We'll include it in the pilot dashboard.

[13:54] Nora: About the pilot timeline — you mentioned deliverables earlier.

[13:59] Maya: Yes to recap: we'll share benchmark spreadsheet + pilot config (Maya). Priya will send security pack. Diego will provide shard configs and instrumentation plan. Lyra will provide sample traces and sign off on pilot traffic percentage.

[14:20] Aisha: One more question: if we observe a tenant causing high eviction churn, can we throttle their cache insert rate?

[14:27] Diego: Yes — admission quotas per tenant or per-tenant insertion rate limits are part of the plan. We can also demote certain tenants to the overflow pool automatically.

[14:40] Tom: For the VPC version, is there an option for zero persistence of values to disk? We want to avoid accidental dumps.

[14:47] Priya: Yes. You can run the cache in-memory-only mode with no persistence on restart; plus we support encrypted ephemeral caches. We'll document it in the security pack.

[15:00] Samir: Any final notes on instrumentation keys we should add to our logs?

[15:05] Diego: Include tenant_id, template_id, cache_lookup=true/false, hit=true/false, model_variant, request_latency_ms, token_savings_estimate. That will let us compute the ROI.

[15:18] Nora: Sounds great. Let's lock dates.

[15:22] Maya: Proposed pilot kick off 2025-10-13, shadow run 2025-10-13 to 10-20, live 10-21 to 11-03. Does that work?

[15:34] Samir: Yes. We need internal approval but tentatively yes.

[15:40] Maya: Perfect. We'll send the materials. Thanks everyone.

[15:46] END OF TRANSCRIPT (note: auto-transcription contains minor mis-labels; some technical terms transcribed phonetically).
